meta.subtitle: Aerospace and defense prime; Q2'26 sales $24.7B up 14%, backlog $289B, guide raised; FY25 net debt $30.5B; 2.0x trailing EBITDA

analystSentiment.commentary: RTX reported Q2'26 results on July 23, 2026: sales of $24.7B, {+ up 14% +} year over year and up 16% organically, adjusted EPS of $1.89, {+ up 21% +}, and a backlog of $289B, {+ up 22% +} year over year. Management raised its 2026 outlook to adjusted EPS of $7.10-$7.25 and free cash flow of $8.50-$8.75B. FY25 net debt was $30.5B, and trailing-twelve-month net debt is 2.0x EBITDA, a moderate level with net debt down since FY23. At $193.12 on September 23, 2026, our call is HOLD, $190-$230. Our $210 Base case holds the multiple the shares carry today on current-year earnings and rolls it onto FY27E EPS of $7.85, so it returns consensus earnings growth and nothing more; that anchor decides the label. The $240 Bull case has the six-week de-rating reverse, and the $155 Bear case has a cost shock stall FY27 earnings. The weighted fair value of $206.50 gives expected upside of +6.9% against bear-case downside of -19.7%, short of the desk's BUY bar.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: RTX Corporation is an aerospace and defense company serving commercial, military and government customers worldwide. It operates through three segments: Collins Aerospace, Pratt & Whitney and Raytheon. Collins Aerospace supplies aerospace and defense products and aftermarket services, including power, environmental, flight-control and cabin systems for civil and military aircraft. Pratt & Whitney supplies aircraft engines for commercial, military, business-jet and general-aviation customers, along with auxiliary power units and aftermarket maintenance, repair and overhaul services. Raytheon provides threat detection, tracking and mitigation capabilities, including sensors and mission systems, for government and commercial customers. Raytheon follows a fiscal calendar, so its Q2'26 ended June 28, 2026, while Collins and Pratt & Whitney use calendar quarter ends. The company was formerly known as Raytheon Technologies Corporation and changed its name to RTX Corporation in July 2023. RTX was incorporated in 1934 and is headquartered in Arlington, Virginia, with more than 180,000 employees and 2025 sales of more than $88 billion.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: RTX pairs a large installed base of engines and aircraft systems with a defense business exposed to munitions and missile-defense demand, and in July management raised its 2026 outlook for adjusted sales, adjusted EPS and free cash flow. We like the business and the visibility its backlog gives. At $193.12 we do not see enough upside to rate it BUY. Our Base case returns roughly consensus earnings growth and no more, for reasons the valuation section sets out. The Bull and Bear cases sit at broadly similar distances from the price, with the Bull somewhat further away and somewhat more likely, so the weighted upside is positive but stays below the desk's BUY bar. HOLD is the result, and it turns on a judgment about the multiple that we flag rather than hide.

catalysts: Backlog: the $289B backlog at the end of Q2'26 gives coverage for the raised 2026 outlook; the growth section covers how it is building.

Defense budget requests: the proposed $1.5 trillion FY2027 defense budget, released April 21, 2026, and a June 24, 2026 supplemental request that includes $21 billion for munitions replenishment could add demand for RTX munitions if Congress funds them.

Golden Dome and munitions funding: the July 4, 2025 Act provides $24.4 billion for the Golden Dome for America project, whose impact on RTX the MD&A says will depend on actual awards, award timelines, mission priorities and future budget determinations, and $25.4 billion for munitions and supply chain resiliency, where the MD&A says RTX is strategically situated to play a key role.
Delivery against the raised outlook: the next quarterly report will show whether the second half supports the July raise.
risks: Valuation: the expected return rests on earnings growth alone, as the valuation section argues.
Leverage: net debt is moderate but meaningful; the balance-sheet discussion covers it.
Pratt & Whitney's Powder Metal Matter, detailed in the risk section.
Limits on capital return from a defense-contractor executive order, detailed in the risk section.
Tariff costs and supply-chain disruption, covered under idiosyncratic and systemic risks.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: Revenue grew from $64.4B in FY21 to $88.6B in FY25, {+ up 9.7% +} in the latest year after {+ 17.1% +} growth in FY24. Operating margin rose from 8.0% in FY21 to 10.5% in FY25, after a trough of 5.2% in FY23 that the excerpts here do not explain. FY25 operating income was $9.3B, net income $6.7B and diluted EPS $4.96. Q2'26 sales were $24.7B; the press release puts growth at 14% year over year and the vendor's quarterly data at 14.5%, and we use the company's 14%. The Q2'26 operating margin was 11.4%, against 11.2% on the trailing twelve months, and the trailing net margin was 8.3%. GAAP EPS was $1.57, {+ up 29% +} from $1.22, and included $0.27 of acquisition accounting adjustments; adjusted EPS was $1.89, {+ up 21% +}. The company credits the growth in adjusted net income to higher adjusted segment operating profit in all three segments. Pratt & Whitney's reported operating profit rose 50%, but the prior-year quarter included an approximately $100 million charge related to a customer bankruptcy, so its adjusted rise of 22% is the cleaner measure. The recovery since FY23 is real, but no year before FY25 in the series had an operating margin above 8.2%, so the multiple depends on RTX holding the higher level for another year.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: RTX ended FY25 with total debt of $37.9B, cash and short-term investments of $8.2B and net debt of $30.5B, against total equity of $67.1B. Debt rose from $31.9B in FY22 to $43.8B in FY23, the year RTX also bought back $12.9B of stock, and has fallen in each year since, to $41.3B in FY24 and the FY25 level above. Net debt followed, down from $37.2B in FY23. The March 9, 2026 proxy statement credits the CFO with paying down $3.4 billion of debt in 2025. On the trailing twelve months, net debt is 2.0x EBITDA. That trailing ratio is not an FY25 figure: measured against FY25 EBITDA of $13.7B, FY25 net debt is somewhat higher than two times. Either way, this is moderate leverage for a company with positive free cash flow in each of the past five years, and the direction is down. Two points temper the read. The MD&A says higher interest rates have increased the cost of borrowing and tightened the availability of capital. And net debt is a fixed claim ahead of shareholders, so any fall in enterprise value takes a somewhat larger share of the equity value. Liquidity is tight but stable: the current ratio was 1.03 at FY25 and 1.01 on the trailing twelve months, within the 0.99 to 1.19 range of the past five years. The balance sheet does not threaten the thesis, but it is not a cushion either, and further paydown is the use of cash that most directly lowers the risk to the equity.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash generation improved in FY25: operating cash flow was $10.6B, capital expenditure -$2.6B and free cash flow $7.9B, a 9.0% free-cash-flow margin, above the 5.6% to 7.9% range of FY21 to FY24. FY25 free cash flow covered dividends paid of -$3.6B, and share repurchases were only -$0.1B, which left room for the debt reduction described under the balance sheet. Q2'26 free cash flow was {+ $2.9B +}, up from {- -$72 million -} a year earlier, on operating cash flow of $3.5B against $458 million and capital expenditure of $0.7B. Because the prior-year quarter was negative, the year-over-year swing flatters the comparison. Management's raised 2026 free-cash-flow outlook of $8.50-$8.75B is the better gauge of the run rate, and it sits above the FY25 level. The trailing free-cash-flow yield is 4.4%.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: At $193.12, RTX trades at 34.0x trailing earnings, 2.8x sales and 19.4x EV/EBITDA; EV/EBITDA includes net debt, so it is the multiple that reflects the whole capital structure. The vendor labels its 26.7x forward multiple next-twelve-month, but at today's price it lines up with consensus FY26E EPS of $7.24, so we treat it as a current-year multiple; on FY27E EPS of $7.85 the multiple is about 24.6x. Consensus FY26E EPS sits inside the company's adjusted EPS outlook of $7.10-$7.25, which suggests it is struck on the adjusted basis. The trailing multiple appears to be on reported (GAAP) earnings, which in Q2'26 included $0.27 of acquisition accounting adjustments, so part of the step-down from trailing to forward may be a difference in basis rather than growth. The pack carries no peer multiples, so this is an absolute read. The 23 analysts covering RTX rate it 15 Buy, 8 Hold and 0 Sell, with a consensus target of $234.41, a median of $240.00 and a range of $200.00 to $265.00. The raised outlook is already in consensus EPS, so at an unchanged current-year multiple the return from here is consensus earnings growth; anything more needs the multiple to rise, which the scenario commentary weighs.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: The six-week de-rating reverses: FY27 EPS reaches or beats consensus FY27E of $7.85, budget and supplemental requests turn into munitions awards, and the current-year multiple returns toward its mid-August level, when the shares closed near the 52-week high of $226.88. The price lands at the Street median target of $240.00.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: The de-rating sticks: RTX delivers the raised 2026 outlook and consensus FY27E EPS, and the 26.7x multiple the shares carry today on current-year earnings holds as the year rolls onto FY27. The return equals consensus EPS growth, with no re-rating.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: A cost shock in FY27: Powder Metal Matter costs, tariffs that cannot be passed through and fixed-price overruns absorb a year of growth, so FY27 EPS stalls at the FY26E consensus of $7.24 instead of reaching consensus FY27E. The current-year multiple compresses to the low twenties, putting the shares near the 52-week low of $155.64.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight the Bull at 25% ($60.00), the Base at 55% ($115.50) and the Bear at 20% ($31.00), for a weighted fair value of $206.50, expected upside of +6.9%, bear-case downside of -19.7% and reward/risk of 0.35x. That derives HOLD, and HOLD is our label. The Base anchor decides it. Holding today's current-year multiple returns only consensus EPS growth from FY26E to FY27E, which sits below the 10% BUY bar at any price, so with this anchor the label stays HOLD unless about seven points of weight move from the Bear to the Bull, taking the Bull to about one-third. We hold the multiple as a view that the de-rating sticks, not as a default, and it is a judgment. The case for it: the shares fell over six weeks with no explanation in the pack, which carries no headlines, so we cannot rule out that the fall reflects information we do not have; and consensus shows growth slowing into FY27, which does not argue for a higher current-year multiple than today's. The case against: the shares closed near the 52-week high in mid-August on the same reported results and the same raised outlook, the lowest Street target sits above the current price, and the consensus target implies a higher multiple than ours. With the Base set at the consensus target and the same weights, the scenarios would derive BUY. The Bear rests on its own story: no FY27 growth is a real but minority outcome, because the MD&A says the company cannot always offset cost increases on fixed-price contracts, while the backlog is still growing. The Bull carries a little more weight than the Bear because the de-rating it reverses happened within the past six weeks. Our $190-$230 target range brackets the $210 Base case.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: The vendor feed reports RTX as a single consolidated line, but the company runs three operating segments, and the Q2'26 press release gives their results; return on sales rose in all three year over year. Collins Aerospace sales were $8,210 million, up 8%, at a 15.9% reported return on sales, with commercial OE up 26% and commercial aftermarket up 10%. Pratt & Whitney sales were $8,889 million, up 16%, at an 8.3% return on sales, with commercial aftermarket up 25% and military up 23%, partly offset by lower commercial OE sales. Raytheon sales were $8,269 million, up 18%, at a 12.6% return on sales, on higher volume on land and air defense systems, naval programs, and air and space defense systems, including Patriot, Standard Missile and AMRAAM. All growth rates are year over year.

moatFactors.name: Aftermarket installed base
moatFactors.body: Many of RTX's aerospace customers are covered by long-term aftermarket service agreements at Collins and Pratt & Whitney, inclusive of spare parts and services. Q2'26 commercial aftermarket sales grew at double-digit rates at both businesses, as the segment detail shows, a recurring stream tied to an installed fleet that is hard for another supplier to displace.

moatFactors.name: Defense incumbency and backlog
moatFactors.body: RTX serves defense customers as a prime contractor or subcontractor on a broad portfolio of programs, with $119B of defense backlog at the end of Q2'26. Multi-year missile programs give visibility, though the government can terminate contracts for convenience.

moatFactors.name: Certification and technology barriers
moatFactors.body: Aircraft engines and defense systems demand certification, qualification and proven performance, which raises barriers to entry. The same demands cut both ways: untested technologies and fixed-price development contracts carry cost-overrun and performance risk that RTX bears.

moatFactors.name: Scale and diversification
moatFactors.body: The scale described in the company overview, spread across three segments and commercial and defense end markets, gives RTX a mix that softens a shock to any single program.

businessMoat.durability: The moat rests on the installed base of engines and aircraft systems that generates long-term aftermarket revenue, and on defense incumbency backed by multi-year programs. Both are durable: aftermarket agreements run for years, and the MD&A describes the defense contracts to design, develop and manufacture complex equipment as long-cycle. The threats to durability are execution and policy rather than displacement, as the quality and fixed-price issues set out in the risk section show. The franchise is wide, but the returns it earns depend on disciplined program execution.

points: Backlog is growing faster than sales: it rose 22% year over year in Q2'26, to $170B commercial and $119B defense, while sales grew 14%, so coverage is building rather than being drawn down. Watch whether backlog keeps outgrowing sales as the large programs ship.

The July 23, 2026 raise lifted the organic-growth outlook to 8-9% from 5-6% and adjusted sales to $95.0-$96.0B from $92.5-$93.5B. Q2'26 organic growth of 16% ran well above the new full-year range, so the second half is the test of whether the raise was cautious.

Consensus puts FY26E revenue at $96.1B and FY27E at $103.2B, with EPS of $7.24 and $7.85, which implies slower growth in FY27 than in FY26. That deceleration is why our Base case does not assume a higher multiple.

The defense funding named among the catalysts maps most directly to Raytheon, whose Q2'26 growth came from the missile programs listed in the segment detail. The March 2026 proxy notes that Raytheon doubled AMRAAM production year over year in 2025 and won a $1.1 billion U.S. Navy contract that will increase AIM-9X Block II production to 2,500 missiles per year; Raytheon's quarterly growth is where new funding would show first.

management.leadership: According to the July 23, 2026 press release, RTX is led by Chairman and CEO Chris Calio, who said demand remains robust and backlog is up 22 percent year over year. The March 9, 2026 proxy statement names Neil G. Mitchill, Jr. as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, with 11 years at RTX; Philip J. Jasper as President, Raytheon, with 34 years; and Shane G. Eddy as President, Pratt & Whitney, with 16 years. Management's stated priorities are executing on the backlog, increasing productivity, expanding capacity and introducing new technologies. The proxy says the CFO oversaw 2025 results that exceeded the adjusted net sales, adjusted EPS and free-cash-flow expectations communicated to investors, despite tariff and supplier headwinds. That record, together with the July raise, supports confidence in execution.
management.capitalAllocation: Since FY23, capital allocation has favored debt reduction and dividends over buybacks. Share repurchases fell from $12.9B in FY23 to $0.4B in FY24 and $0.1B in FY25, while the deleveraging described under the balance sheet proceeded. The proxy says that in 2025 RTX invested $7.7 billion in company- and customer-funded research and development and capital expenditures, increased its annual dividend rate by 7.9% and returned over $3.6 billion of capital to shareowners. The quarterly dividend rose from $0.63 to $0.68 per share in the second quarter of 2025, and the current dividend yield is 1.53%. At today's moderate leverage, we think paydown ahead of buybacks is the right order. The executive-order risk to distributions, set out in the risk section, is the one policy constraint on this plan.
management.governance: Governance rests on the DEF 14A proxy statement dated March 9, 2026. Under RTX's Director Independence Policy and NYSE listing standards, a majority of directors must be independent; the Board determined that, other than Mr. Calio as a current RTX employee, each nominee for the 2026 Annual Meeting satisfies the independence criteria. Directors complete an annual questionnaire on relationships and transactions that may affect independence. Related-person transactions above $120,000 require Governance Committee review. On pay, the HCC Committee approved a 164% of target performance factor for Corporate and a $7.5 million 2026 LTI award for the CFO, an amount above the market median for his role. The structure is conventional and the board is independent apart from the CEO; above-median awards in a year of above-expectation results do not concern us. The MD&A adds that the Russian government has imposed counter-sanctions targeting certain members of RTX's management team and Board of Directors.

idiosyncratic: Pratt & Whitney Powder Metal Matter: in 2023 Pratt & Whitney determined that a rare condition in powder metal used to manufacture certain engine parts requires accelerated inspection of the PW1100 GTF fleet that powers the A320neo family. The excerpts carry no cost estimate, so the size of any further charge is unknown.

Fixed-price contract exposure: under firm fixed-price contracts RTX carries the burden of cost overruns, and under fixed-price incentive contracts it carries all overruns above the ceiling price; inflation, tariffs and supply constraints could produce losses it cannot always offset through pricing.

Tariffs: RTX has paid approximately $0.5 billion of IEEPA tariffs and has submitted refund claims, which it will recognize if and when approved; the U.S. government appealed the refund order on June 2, 2026, and new and revised tariffs imposed after the Supreme Court ruling may apply to products RTX imports.

Capital-return limits: an executive order may limit distributions, share repurchases and executive compensation incentives during periods of defense-contractor underperformance under U.S. government contracts, and the company warns that such a limit could adversely affect the share price.
Program execution: contract terminations for convenience or default, performance delays and cost overruns on advanced programs could impair results and future award opportunities.
risks.systemic: Systemic risk centers on U.S. government defense spending and the macro environment. U.S. government sales are a significant portion of consolidated sales, and budget changes, continuing resolutions or shutdowns could delay awards, payments and new program starts. The MD&A cites inflation, interest rates, foreign-currency movements and volatile global trade policy as sources of uncertainty for cost and demand. The global supply chain remains constrained, and management expects disruptions to continue, affecting raw materials including certain rare earth elements, microelectronics and certain commodities. Commercial aerospace demand is tied to revenue passenger miles, the financial health of airlines and the performance of airframers, so a downturn in air travel would weigh on Collins and Pratt & Whitney. These factors sit largely outside the company's control and inform the Bear weight.

body: We rate RTX HOLD with a target range of $190 to $230 against the $193.12 price of September 23, 2026. The business is executing well and the backlog supports the Base case, but as the valuation section argues, the price leaves the expected return close to consensus earnings growth: the weighted fair value of $206.50 gives expected upside of +6.9% against bear-case downside of -19.7%.

The call is close on price. On these scenarios, a pullback of a few percent from today's price would derive BUY: the reward/risk test clears first, and the expected-upside test, which binds, clears a little lower, and a price modestly above our Base case would derive SELL. The page's price history shows a steady decline over the six weeks to September 23 from closes near the 52-week high, and no source in the pack explains it; on these scenarios the mid-August closes would have derived SELL and the early-September closes HOLD. We would raise the Base case if the company lifts its 2026 outlook again or consensus FY27E EPS moves above $7.85 while the price lags. We would move weight to the Bear case if segment margins give back the Q2'26 gains or the outlook is cut.
